The Threat of Race, Measured

The AI models that now power image search have learned to identify race — and to couple it to words like threatening, primitive, and intelligent. We measured those couplings across seven museum collections, traced each one to the model, the depicted scene, or the curation — and built a repair with mathematical guarantees.

Paper (PDF)Code & data

1 · How images are found nowEvery search is a reading

When you search a photo library, a shopping site, or a museum's online collection, a single kind of AI model increasingly does the looking: a vision‑language model. The model is the reader; what it writes down is an embedding — a long list of numbers summarizing everything it saw in the image, placed in an invisible space so that an image sits near the words that describe it. The search itself never looks at the pictures again: it runs entirely on these embeddings. And it is no longer only people doing the searching — AI agents that go looking for images on our behalf use this same machinery as their eyes.

That trick is why you can type "a quiet street after rain" and get exactly that, with no tags or catalogue labels. But it means the model's sense of which words sit near which pictures is quietly steering what surfaces first and what stays buried. If the model has learned — from the billions of web images it trained on — that certain people sit near certain words, every search built on it inherits that association, automatically and at scale.

We audited the strongest open model of this kind, SigLIP‑2, cataloguing the 226,088 objects of the Harvard Art Museums.

2 · What we foundThe map of couplings

We asked a simple question, eighty ways: when the model reads an artwork as depicting a person of a particular group, does its reading of that person lean toward a trait word — and always in the same direction? We call a consistent lean a coupling. Every candidate had to survive two independent ways of measuring, and hold not just at Harvard but in four more encyclopedic museums we measured the same way — the Met, the Art Institute of Chicago, the Cleveland Museum of Art, and Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum. Our instruments were checked against 782 human judgments along the way.

20
The number of race stereotype couplings we verified.
primitive
attaches most strongly to African and Indigenous subjects — the two groups the term has historically been used against

lazy

8 of 8

The couplings mirror stereotype content documented in human subjects for a century — the model has not invented a new prejudice; it has absorbed and sharpened an old one.

3 · See the collection as the model sees it50,000 artworks, one reading each

Below, each dot is one Harvard artwork, placed so that works the model reads similarly sit near each other. The color is the model's skin-tone reading of the work — darker to lighter. The gradient you see is the structure the rest of this page is about.

4 · Whose bias is it?The model, the scene, or the museum

A coupling in a museum's search can come from three places. The model's own prior: it reads the association off a person alone, no context needed. The model reading people through the scenes they are depicted in — a prison scene, a labor scene — which happens in any collection that holds such scenes, however well curated. And the collection's particular mix: not what is inside any one image, but which images the museum holds at all — a mix that can amplify the rest or null it. The three are connected, of course: the scene is only there because someone collected it. But we separate them because each has a different owner, and a different repair. The paper's central experiment does the separating.

We re-ran every measurement in two collections assembled expressly to depict Black subjects with dignity — W. E. B. Du Bois's 1900 Paris Exposition albums and the National Museum of African American History and Culture. Among depicted people, dignity curation works: the threatening- and criminal-couplings vanish there, and ugly and unintelligent reverse. Then we removed collections entirely, testing the model on standardized studio photographs of faces: threatening and the competence cluster reproduce on bare faces — those belong to the model — while primitive and criminal do not, needing the depicted scene to exist.

5 · The repairCut the coupling, keep the collection

The repair is one linear operation with a proof behind it: inside the model's small subspace of trait readings, remove exactly the component that predicts identity — nothing else. Identity stays searchable. Mediums, periods, and styles stay put. The correlation between trait words and identity readings is what dies. We call it the de‑coupler.

Press the button. The dots are 6,000 works the model reads as depicting people; the bars are the exact measurements. Hover any dot to see the artwork.

The exact numbers: correlation of each trait reading with skin tone

Two bars move the wrong way (wealthy, civilized). We show them deliberately: this edit was fit to protect the nine named race categories, and skin tone was held out as a test. Removing named categories can shift bias into directions the labels miss — measured here at its worst, r = 0.14. Adding skin tone to the protected set closes it to zero at the cost of one extra dimension. Coverage is something we measure, not assume.

6 · What the repair cannot doHonesty about limits

The de-coupler repairs geometry — the model's learned bias. It cannot repair what a collection contains. For the query "a criminal," works read as depicting brown people surface at five times their share of the collection, and the de-coupler does not reduce that; the association runs through the scenes themselves — banditry prints, prison scenes — not through the trait geometry. Erasing the geometry actually unmasks the collection's own contribution. This is a surprising result, and a revealing one: the statistical averaging at the heart of these vision models can amplify some biases and occlude others at the same time — so removing one layer of bias can bring another into view.

And some couplings are not errors at all. A "threatening × Black" association inside an archive documenting racial violence is that archive's meaning — testimony, not stereotype. That is why the deployed tool routes every erasure target, with its retrieved examples, through a curator, and stores every edit reversibly. Statistics cannot tell a stereotype from testimony. People can.

A note on the title. It echoes David Theo Goldberg's The Threat of Race: Reflections on Racial Neoliberalism (Wiley-Blackwell, 2009), which argues that contemporary societies re-encode racism structurally even while declaring themselves past it. This study recognizes that conceptualization and gives it a measurement: the models that now mediate how images are found formalize structural racism in exactly the way Goldberg described — encoding marginalized populations as perpetual threats within their latent space, and imposing that encoding, automatically and at scale, on every search built above it. Goldberg named the ideology; here it can be measured inside the machine.

The Threat of Race, Measured — Bridget Mullen et al., 2026.
